# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Contemporary Narrative Review

### Introduction and Epidemiology
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) that uniquely affects women of childbearing age. It is defined by the development of heart failure during the last month of pregnancy or within the first few postpartum months, in the absence of an alternative identifiable cause, with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45% [1,2]. While historically considered rare, the global epidemiology of PPCM reveals significant geographical disparities [2,3]. A disproportionately high prevalence is documented in regions like Haiti and South Africa, as well as among women of African ancestry in the United States [4]. Major risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestations, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and black race [4,5].

### Pathophysiology
The underlying etiology of PPCM was long enigmatic, but recent molecular advances have established a "two-hit" mechanism combining vascular/hormonal insults and genetic predisposition. During late pregnancy, elevated oxidative stress in the myocardium drives the activation of cathepsin D, which cleaves full-length prolactin into a toxic 16-kDa anti-angiogenic, pro-apoptotic, and pro-inflammatory fragment [6]. This fragment disrupts the microvasculature, inducing endothelial injury and subsequent cardiomyocyte dysfunction [6]. Simultaneously, late-pregnancy placental secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) impairs vascular homeostasis, contributing to an systemic angiogenic imbalance that exacerbates myocardial stress [7].

Recent genetic sequencing has also identified a shared genetic architecture between PPCM and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [8,9]. Approximately 10% to 15% of PPCM patients carry pathogenic truncating mutations in the titin gene (*TTN*), suggesting that pregnancy unmasks an underlying genetic vulnerability to hemodynamic stress [9]. Downregulation of cardiac STAT3 and upregulation of microRNAs, particularly microRNA-146a, act as key molecular mediators of this pathway [10]. Ultimately, this interplay of systemic angiogenic imbalance, hormonal cleavage, and genetic susceptibility leads to the clinical manifestations of PPCM [11].

### Diagnosis and Clinical Presentation
Diagnosing PPCM is challenging because early symptoms—such as dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, and peripheral edema—frequently mimic the normal physiological changes of late pregnancy and the postpartum period, leading to frequent diagnostic delays [12,13]. A high index of suspicion is required. The initial workup should include an electrocardiogram, serum natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP), and transthoracic echocardiography [14,15]. Echocardiography is the gold standard for confirming an LVEF < 45%, establishing chamber dimensions, and ruling out other cardiovascular pathologies [14]. International registries, such as the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) EURObservational Research Programme (EORP), have highlighted that standardized diagnostic algorithms drastically reduce time-to-diagnosis and improve clinical outcomes [12,16,17].

### Management Strategies
Therapeutic management of PPCM is dictated by the timing of presentation (antepartum versus postpartum). During pregnancy, standard guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) must be altered to protect the fetus. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are strictly contraindicated due to risk of teratogenicity, fetotoxicity, and neonatal renal failure [15,18]. Instead, afterload reduction is achieved using hydralazine and nitrates, while beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective agents like metoprolol succinate) and loop diuretics are utilized for symptom control [15].

Postpartum, standard GDMT for HFrEF can be fully instituted [20,21]. Based on pathophysiology, the dopamine agonist bromocriptine has emerged as a disease-specific therapy to block pituitary prolactin release [18,19]. Proof-of-concept and randomized trials demonstrate that adding bromocriptine to standard heart failure regimens accelerates LVEF recovery and reduces composite clinical endpoints [18,19]. Because bromocriptine increases thromboembolic risk, it must be combined with prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation (using heparin or warfarin), particularly if LVEF is under 30% [20]. 

In cases of acute cardiogenic shock, inotropic support (e.g., levosimendan, dobutamine) and advanced mechanical circulatory support, such as a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), serve as critical bridges to recovery or durable ventricular assist device (VAD) implantation [22,23,24].

### Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies
Unlike other non-ischemic cardiomyopathies, PPCM carries a relatively favorable prognosis, with over 50% to 70% of patients achieving full recovery of LVEF (≥ 50%) within six months of diagnosis [13,25]. However, the risk of recurrence during subsequent pregnancies remains a formidable challenge. Women with persistent left ventricular dysfunction should be strongly counseled against future pregnancies due to high risks of clinical relapse, severe heart failure, and maternal mortality [26,27]. For patients who fully recover LVEF, subsequent pregnancies still carry a 20% to 30% risk of recurrence [28,29]. Management of future pregnancies requires extensive preconception counseling, multidisciplinary care, and close cardiovascular monitoring through gestation and the high-risk postpartum period [28,30].
